2_Introduction: By refining specific fabrication parameters, a perovskite solar cell was fabricated, culminating in performance metrics including a PCE of 0.76%, FF of 26.55%, Voc of 0.16 V, and Jsc of 17.66 mA/cm². The perovskite composition was Cs0.05MA0.16FA0.79Pb1I2.9Br0.1, and the initial stock perovskite solution was 1.75 mol/L. The perovskite solutions were spin-coated onto the substrate at 1000 rpm for 10 s and 5000 rpm for 40 s. When the countdown was 10 s, 120 µL CB serving as antisolvent was dropped onto the substrates. The samples were subsequently annealed on a hotplate at 100 °C for 30 min. Spectral analysis indicates that, upon the onset of annealing, the film reaches the explosive nucleation point at 8.6 seconds, at which the photoluminescence (PL) intensity attains its maximum. Following this peak, the PL intensity decreases to 30% of its maximum value, with an average decay slope of 5.604583333.
3_Result_Discussion: The Cs₀.₀₅MA₀.₁₆FA₀.₇₉PbI₂.₉Br₀.₁ perovskite layer—engineered with a carefully tuned A-site cation mixture to optimize Goldschmidt tolerance factor (~0.98) and suppress phase segregation while mitigating halide vacancy formation and Pb²⁺-associated deep traps—undergoes highly sensitive crystallization kinetics governed by the interplay of precursor concentration (1.75 mol/L), dual-speed spin-coating (1000 rpm/10 s for wet-film formation followed by 5000 rpm/40 s for rapid solvent expulsion), and precisely timed antisolvent quenching (120 µL chlorobenzene at 10 s countdown), which collectively modulates nucleation density, intermediate solvate phase stability, and grain boundary coalescence; this protocol yields a metastable yet kinetically trapped film that, upon thermal annealing at 100 °C for 30 min, undergoes explosive nucleation at 8.6 s—evidenced by the sharp PL intensity maximum—signifying the critical onset of crystal lattice ordering and excitonic delocalization, after which the subsequent 70% decay in PL intensity with an average slope of 5.60 reveals rapid non-radiative recombination pathways arising from residual undercoordinated Pb–I bonds, unpassivated halide vacancies, and interfacial trap states at grain boundaries and substrate interfaces, corroborating insufficient defect suppression and poor interfacial energy alignment in the absence of molecular passivators or surface modifiers; critically, the absence of any SAMs, additives, or passivating agents in the described fabrication means no anchoring-group-mediated interfacial dipole formation, no Lewis base coordination to undercoordinated Pb²⁺, no halide vacancy filling via ammonium or phosphonium groups, and no strain relaxation via bifunctional ligands—leaving the perovskite/substrate interface electronically “raw” and morphologically heterogeneous, as further implied by the steep PL decay and lack of spectral narrowing or lifetime elongation typically associated with suppressed trap-assisted recombination; consequently, the resulting device suffers from severe voltage losses due to interfacial recombination, poor charge extraction efficiency from disordered grain networks, and substantial series resistance stemming from incomplete film coverage and high defect density, culminating in Voc = 0.16 V, Jsc = 17.66 mA/cm², FF = 26.55%, and PCE = 0.76%.
